title: Europe's Deadly Heatwave Puts All Italian Cities on Red Alert as Energy Crisis Deepens
excerpt: Italy issues unprecedented top-level heat warning for all 27 major cities as Austria sets temperature records, Hungary shuts down its nuclear plant, and the EU counts over €15 billion in wildfire damage.
body:
• Italy placed all 27 major cities on red alert for the first time, warning of a potential health emergency from Palermo to Bolzano.
  • Austria set an all-time temperature record of 41.2°C (106.2°F), while Hungary turned off lights at parliament and the Buda Castle to conserve energy.
  • Danube water levels have forced Hungary and Romania to shut down nuclear reactors, triggering a regional energy crisis across Central Europe.
  • EU wildfire damage this summer has exceeded €15 billion, with the bloc pledging to push member states to increase spending on fire prevention.

Italy took the unprecedented step on Thursday of placing all its major cities on the highest level of health alert as a punishing heatwave continued to grip central and southern Europe, triggering an energy crisis that has forced Hungary and Romania to switch off lights and shut down nuclear power plants.

The red alert issued by Italy's Health Ministry stretched from Palermo on the southern island of Sicily to Bolzano in the mountainous north — a warning indicating prolonged high temperatures that pose a serious health risk to the entire population. Temperatures topped 42.8°C (109°F) in Bagnacavallo, near Ravenna, in the Emilia-Romagna region.

Records Shattered Across Central Europe

Austria recorded its hottest day in history on Wednesday when temperatures reached 41.2°C (106.2°F) in Bad Deutsch-Altenburg, near the Slovak border, according to national weather service GeoSphere Austria. The previous record of 41.0°C had been set just one day earlier in Vienna.

Europe — the world's fastest-warming continent — has been battered by successive heatwaves this summer, with France and Spain particularly hard hit by destructive wildfires in recent weeks. The European Union said the economic cost of this summer's blazes had already exceeded €15 billion ($17.3 billion).

"We try to avoid going out during the hottest part of the day and instead go out in the evening or early in the morning."

— Gianni Arlotta, tourist visiting Rome from Trieste

Nuclear Plants Forced Offline by Danube Crisis

The heatwave has exposed critical vulnerabilities in Europe's energy infrastructure. Record-low water levels on the Danube have forced Hungary to largely shut down its sole nuclear power plant at Paks, which relies on the river for cooling. The shutdown has stretched the country's power supply capacity to its limits.

Hungary switched off decorative and non-essential lighting at state institutions — including its parliament, most of the Buda Castle, and the Chain Bridge — at night to conserve energy. Prime Minister Péter Magyar thanked citizens for cutting power consumption but warned the next few days would be critical.

In Romania, two nuclear reactors at the Cernavoda plant were forced offline last month due to low Danube levels, prompting a nationwide state of emergency over declining electricity production. The military carried out controlled explosions on the Danube's Bala canal this week to divert water toward the plant. Bucharest dimmed street lights by a third and switched off lighting at landmark buildings and museums.

Slovenia's only nuclear plant at Krško began reducing reactor output due to exceptionally high temperatures and low flows on the Sava River.

Wildfires, Drought, and Agricultural Damage

In Albania, wildfires in the southern Mallakaster region forced the evacuation of about 15 families. Greece continued battling a major blaze that burned thousands of hectares of farmland near a popular holiday destination northwest of Athens. In Moldova, President Maia Sandu urged residents to cut electricity and water use during peak hours.

The heat is hammering agriculture across the continent. Britain's cereal harvest is on track to be the worst since comparable records began in 1984, as crops wither after one of the driest and hottest spring-summer periods on record. Low water levels on Germany's Rhine have disrupted commodity shipping, with vessels sailing part-loaded and freight costs rising.

What Indian Travellers Should Know

The heatwave poses significant risks for the hundreds of thousands of Indian tourists and students currently in Europe during peak summer season. Several countries have issued health advisories urging people to avoid outdoor activities during afternoon hours. Public events, including Pope Leo's weekly general audience, have been moved indoors. Travellers are advised to carry water, seek air-conditioned shelters during midday, and monitor local emergency alerts.

What's Next

Forecasters expect the heatwave to persist through the weekend across much of southern and central Europe, with Budapest bracing for temperatures near 40°C for consecutive days — only the second time in the city's recorded history. The EU's environment commissioner told Reuters the bloc would push member countries to increase spending on wildfire prevention measures.
